metadata.title: Pay vs. Prices: Who Is Winning?
metadata.section: Section C: Labor Dynamics, Wages & Consumer Prices
metadata.visual_form: Tug-of-war: pay pulls one way, prices the other

series_manifest.label: Real Buying Power (Green = Winning, Red = Losing)

events.label: Prices fall in recession: buying power up 4.3%
Low-paid job losses lift the average wage

explanation.summary: A raise only helps if it is bigger than the rise in prices. This chart compares the yearly change in average hourly pay with inflation. The difference is the change in real buying power: green when pay wins, red when prices win.
explanation.methodology: Average hourly earnings of all private-sector employees (BLS CES0500000003), year-over-year change. Inflation is the year-over-year change in CPI-U (BLS). Real buying power = pay growth minus inflation. The hourly earnings series starts in 2006, so the chart starts in March 2007.

key_findings.title: July 2008: Gas Eats the Raise
key_findings.description: Pay was up 3.2% but prices were up 5.6%, so buying power fell 2.5%.
key_findings.significance: Expensive gas made a normal raise feel like a pay cut.

key_findings.title: June 2022: The Worst Squeeze on the Chart
key_findings.description: The average raise was 5.4%, the fastest in years, but inflation was 9.1%. Buying power fell 3.7%.
key_findings.significance: Big raises still lost to bigger price increases.

key_findings.title: May 2023: Raises Win Again
key_findings.description: For the first time in two years, pay growth (4.4%) beat inflation (4.0%). As of August 2026 inflation (3.4%) is slightly above pay growth (3.1%) again.
key_findings.significance: Workers won back buying power for about three years; that gain has now stopped.
